title: Hyper-parameter heatmap per solver: how sensitive is each solver to its settings?
summary: Every solver has settings. A heat map of success rate over two settings, one panel per solver on a shared colour scale, shows how sensitive each solver is, and whether its good region is wide or a needle.

media.alt: Three side-by-side 5 by 5 heat maps titled solver A, B and C, each with step scale p1 across and population p2 up; cell values printed; a shared viridis colour bar from 0 to 1; solver B has a broad bright region, A and C a single bright cell each.
media.caption: Reference render of class F7.3 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How sensitive is each solver to its settings?
read_the_figure.axes: Each panel: p1 (step scale: 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2) across and p2 (population: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16) up; categorical, unevenly spaced values. Colour: success rate from 0 to 1, shared by all panels.
look_at: Which solver has the largest bright region, and which a single bright cell?
Do the peaks of the three solvers sit at the same settings?
How much does the success rate drop one step away from the peak?
Are the colour scale and the printed values the same in every panel?
as_drawn: Solver A peaks at 0.93 at (0.2, 8) and has only 5 of 25 cells at or above 0.5, mean 0.21. Solver B peaks at 0.96 at (0.5, 4) and has 21 of 25 cells at or above 0.5, mean 0.66. Solver C peaks at 0.96 at (1, 2), has 1 cell at or above 0.5 and mean 0.12.
The three peaks are at different settings, so no single setting is best for all solvers.
All three panels use one colour bar (0 to 1) and print the value in every cell, so panels can be compared by colour and by number.
The axes carry only five values each, unevenly spaced, so a narrow peak between grid values could be missed.
read_the_figure.proves: If a solver has a wide bright region it is robust to its settings; a single bright cell means that the good performance needs careful tuning. The map says nothing about settings outside the grid.
if_wrong: Different colour scales in the panels: the reader compares brightness across incompatible scales.
No cell values: small differences between similar colours cannot be read.
One run per cell: each value is noisy and the maximum is biased upwards.
must_check: shared colour scale across solvers: the whole point is a comparison between solvers, so the colours must mean the same thing in each panel.
cell values: colour is a coarse channel; the printed number lets the reader see the real differences and the size of the drop-off.

terms.meaning: A setting of the solver chosen before the run (for example a step scale or population size).
The fraction of runs that reach a stated target within the budget.
How little the performance changes when the settings move away from the best values.
The uncertainty of a success rate from n runs.
One mapping from value to colour used for every panel, so panels are comparable.

remember: Success rate from n runs has standard error sqrt(p (1 - p) / n).
The best of many noisy cells is biased upwards.
A wide plateau means robust; a needle means tuning-dependent.
One colour scale for all panels.
Print the values in the cells.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each small square is one pair of settings; colour encodes the success rate (dark purple 0, yellow 1) and the number inside repeats it to two decimals, in black or white for legibility. The three panels share both axes' labels, the vertical axis only on the first, and one colour bar on the right.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: a solver that works only for one exact setting is fragile; one that works for a wide range of settings is easy to use. A heat map shows that shape at a glance, a plateau against a spike. Putting the solvers side by side on one scale lets you compare not only their best values but how much care each needs, which a single 'best result' number hides.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The best cell of each solver is a maximum over noisy values, and so is optimistic: with 25 cells of true rate 0.5 and 50 runs each, the best cell typically reads 0.64. The grid is coarse and its spacing uneven, so a narrow peak can fall between values. A reader may compare the peaks, 0.93 and 0.96, which are nearly equal, instead of the breadth, which differs a lot. And success is relative to a fixed budget and target.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A line plot of success against one setting with error bars at fixed other settings gives the uncertainty. A single summary such as the area above a threshold, or the fraction of cells above 0.5, puts breadth into one number per solver. A sensitivity analysis (F8.5) ranks the settings by influence.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a fourth row of small bars showing the fraction of cells at or above 0.5 for each solver, outline the best cell in each panel, and print the number of runs per cell and its standard error in the corner.

steps.title: Uncertainty of one cell
steps.note: Two cells must differ by about 2 SE of the difference, here 0.2 for n = 50, before the difference is convincing.

steps.title: Breadth as one number
steps.note: From the printed values: A 5/25 = 0.20, B 21/25 = 0.84, C 1/25 = 0.04.

steps.title: Bias of the best cell
steps.note: Simulated: 25 cells of true rate 0.5 and 50 runs each give an expected maximum of 0.64.

worked.title: Reading the sensitivity maps of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What are the peak and the breadth (cells at or above 0.5) of each solver? (2) Which solver would you choose if you could not tune? (3) How different must two cells be to be convincing if each uses 50 runs?

solution.text: (1) Read the printed values and count.
(2) Solver B: it is above 0.5 in 21 of 25 cells, so most settings work, while A and C have a good result only near their tuned cell.
(3) The standard error of a rate near 0.5 with 50 runs is 0.07; for a difference of two cells it is about 0.1, so a gap should exceed about 0.2.

worked.answer: A: 0.93 and 5 cells; B: 0.96 and 21 cells; C: 0.96 and 1 cell. Choose B if you cannot tune. With 50 runs per cell, differences below about 0.2 between two cells are not convincing.

analyze.q: Solver C has the same peak as B. Why is it a worse choice for a user who has no time to tune?
The peaks of the three solvers are at different cells. What does that say about comparing solvers at one fixed setting?
A cell reads 0.96 for solver B. How would you check that it is not a lucky value?

evaluate.q: Is the map enough to declare B the best solver?
evaluate.hint: Other problems, budget, cost per evaluation.

Redraw with a log-spaced axis and finer grid near the peaks.

checks.q: What does a wide bright region tell you about a solver?
checks.answer: That it is robust: many settings work well, so it needs little tuning.

checks.q: A cell has a success rate of 0.8 from 100 runs. What is its standard error?
The best cells of two solvers read 0.93 and 0.96. Why is it unsafe to call the second better?
checks.answer: Each is a maximum over noisy cells and has a standard error of a few hundredths, so the difference of 0.03 is within the noise; the breadth and repeated runs tell more.
